final_recommendation: The room converged on a trilateral USMCA package signed by end of business: 75% RVC with five-year mandatory phase-in, dual labor enforcement reports (independent auditors report directly, Mexico publishes parallel records), Class 6/7 dairy phased over five years, Chapter 19 intact, and sunset converted from hard expiration to six-year review mechanism with no automatic kill-switch.
minority_objections: Mexico initially resisted independent auditors reporting directly without co-signing authority, viewing it as sovereignty erosion
Dairy/ag initially demanded full market access before accepting limited Class 6/7 phased concession
Supply chain manufacturers expressed persistent concern that Congress might rewrite sunset language in committee markup despite written assurances
key_conflicts: Labor enforcement inspection protocol: Congress/labor demanded independent auditors with direct reporting vs. Mexico's insistence on co-inspection sovereignty and co-signing findings
Dairy market access: U.S. ag demanded expanded access to supply-managed categories vs. Canada's red line on dairy
Sunset clause: Business uncertainty over hard expiration vs. Congress desire for kill-switch vs. Canada/Mexico need for stability
key_concessions: Mexico accepted dual-report framework: independent auditors report directly to panel, Mexico's ministry publishes parallel inspection records same day (sovereignty preserved through transparency, not veto)
Canada accepted limited dairy concession: Class 6 and 7 phased access over five years with domestic support locked
U.S./Congress accepted sunset conversion from hard kill-switch to six-year review mechanism with no automatic termination
All parties accepted 75% RVC with five-year mandatory phase-in (not aspirational target)
red_lines: Canada: Chapter 19 dispute settlement must remain intact (stated multiple times, never compromised)
Canada: Dairy supply management cannot be fully dismantled (held firm, accepted only limited Class 6/7 phased access)
Congress/Labor: Independent auditors must report violations directly to panel without Mexican ministry veto power over findings or remedies
Mexico: Labor inspection cannot be fully unilateral foreign enforcement on Mexican soil (resolved via dual-report compromise)
Industry: Sunset cannot be hard automatic termination creating investment uncertainty (resolved via review mechanism)
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: Post-signature congressional committee markup risk: supply chain manufacturers repeatedly warned that Congress might rewrite sunset language despite written assurances, but USTR dismissed this as resolved
Parliamentary ratification in Canada: Canada minister raised Parliament backing as conditional on enforcement details, but this was not revisited after labor enforcement compromise

Compliance cost and supplier reorganization timeline: auto industry flagged capex decisions and retooling timelines, but five-year phase-in was treated as sufficient without detailed implementation planning
downstream_risk_variables: Congressional committee markup of sunset review language
Mexican labor ministry capacity and political will to implement dual-report inspection regime
Canadian parliamentary ratification vote given limited dairy concession
Auto supply chain compliance costs and actual timeline to meet 75% RVC within five years
Enforcement of 90-day automatic suspension mechanism in practice
uncertainty_notes: While the text was declared 'locked' and signed by end of business, several participants (supply chain, auto industry) expressed concern that Congress might reinterpret or rewrite sunset language during committee markup. The dual-report labor enforcement framework resolved the immediate impasse but left implementation details (audit frequency, facility selection, remedy escalation) unspecified. Canada's parliamentary ratification path was assumed but not confirmed with vote counts.

marker_evidence.auto_rules_bottleneck: 75% RVC and five-year phase-in drove multiple rounds of negotiation; auto industry demanded written confirmation before committing capex; USTR used RVC lock-down as ultimatum to force Canada's entry
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_key: Labor enforcement inspection protocol (independent auditors vs. co-signing) was the primary R3-R4 deadlock; Congress stated 'this deal dies in committee' without direct reporting; dual-report compromise was the breakthrough that enabled signature
marker_evidence.canada_dairy_final_issue: Dairy access was Canada's stated red line ('off the table'); U.S. ag demanded it as trade-off for labor enforcement; limited Class 6/7 phased concession was the specific compromise that brought Canada into the package
marker_evidence.dispute_settlement_canada_redline: Canada stated Chapter 19 must stay intact multiple times and made it conditional for signing; USTR accepted it as part of the package, but it did not drive the negotiation outcome—it was preserved, not negotiated
marker_evidence.sunset_to_review_compromise: Sunset clause conversion from hard kill-switch to six-year review mechanism was explicitly demanded by industry (capex uncertainty), accepted by Congress, and written into the final text as a condition for signature
marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Congress repeatedly stated enforcement language must satisfy committee or 'deal dies'; dairy/ag demanded confirmation of votes; supply chain warned of markup risk; ratification constraints shaped labor enforcement compromise and sunset language
marker_evidence.supply_chain_adjustment: Supply chain manufacturers raised capex hold decisions and compliance cost concerns; auto industry flagged retooling timelines; but five-year phase-in was accepted as sufficient and did not block the deal
marker_evidence.us_mexico_first_pressures_canada: USTR explicitly threatened bilateral ratification without Canada ('you're getting this or I move forward with Mexico alone'); this ultimatum forced Canada to accept dairy concession and enter the trilateral package
